ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: in the figure, the large rhombus is ABCD, BD connects vertices B and D of the large rhombus, and is a diagonal of the large rhombus; the small rhombus is BFDE, in which B and D are also opposite vertices, so BD is also the diagonal of the small rhombus BFDE connecting opposite vertices. Then reason: let the side length of the large rhombus ABCD be s. Because ABCD is a rhombus, AB=AD=s; and because ∠BAD=60°, triangle ABD has two equal sides and the included angle is 60°, therefore △ABD is an equilateral triangle, so BD=s. Since ABCD and BFDE are similar, the small rhombus also has an acute angle of 60°. Let the side length of the small rhombus BFDE be t. In a rhombus with an acute angle of 60°, the length of the long diagonal connecting the two acute-angle vertices is t√3. In the small rhombus, BD is exactly this long diagonal, so t√3=s, that is, t/s=1/√3. The area ratio of similar figures is equal to the square of the side length ratio, therefore area(BFDE)=24·(1/√3)^2=24/3=8.

raw_record.question_text: Rhombus $ABCD$ is similar to rhombus $BFDE$. The area of rhombus $ABCD$ is 24, and $\angle BAD = 60^\circ$. What is the area of rhombus $BFDE$?

method.method_draft: Use the shared segment BD to relate the side lengths. From the image, BD is a diagonal of the large rhombus ABCD and also the diagonal joining opposite vertices B and D of the smaller rhombus BFDE. Let the side length of ABCD be s. Since ABCD is a rhombus and angle BAD is 60°, triangle ABD has AB = AD and included angle 60°, so triangle ABD is equilateral; therefore BD = s. By similarity, BFDE also has 60° acute angles. In a 60° rhombus of side length t, the diagonal joining the acute vertices has length t√3. In BFDE, BD is that long diagonal, so t√3 = s, hence t/s = 1/√3. Areas of similar figures scale by the square of the side ratio, so area(BFDE) = 24 · (1/√3)^2 = 8.
